topics.briefing: Elizabeth I was Henry VIII’s daughter, but she only reached the English throne because her younger half-brother Edward VI and older half-sister Mary I both died without children. Her 44-year reign became known as the Elizabethan Era, a golden age of Shakespeare’s plays and English voyages at sea, though she famously never married or named an heir. When Spain’s King Philip II sent his “Invincible” Armada to invade England in 1588, storms and the English navy sent it home defeated instead.

tossups.r: She gave that speech at Tilbury while England still feared invasion by Spain’s “Invincible” Armada. For 10 points, name this English queen, the daughter of Henry VIII, known as the “Virgin Queen.”

tossups.p: This monarch’s principal secretary, William Cecil, Lord Burghley, guided most of her foreign policy, while her spymaster Francis Walsingham foiled the Throckmorton and Babington Plots against her. This monarch’s navy, aided by commanders like Francis Drake, defeated an invasion fleet sent by Spain’s King Philip II in 1588.
tossups.r: She died childless in 1603, ending the Tudor line and passing the crown to James Stuart. For 10 points, name this final Tudor monarch of England, half-sister of Mary I.

tossups.p: Pope Pius V excommunicated this monarch in 1570, encouraging Catholic plots to replace her with her cousin and prisoner, Mary, Queen of Scots. This monarch finally signed the execution warrant for that rival royal in 1587, despite years of hesitation.
tossups.r: She never named an heir of her own, having refused every suitor who proposed marriage. For 10 points, name this unmarried English queen nicknamed the “Virgin Queen.”

tossups.p: Robert Cecil had to prepare in secret for this monarch’s death because she refused to name a successor. Early in her reign, this monarch reversed her half-sister’s Catholic restoration by passing a new Act of Supremacy in 1559.
tossups.r: That act made her Supreme Governor of the Church of England. For 10 points, name this Tudor queen, daughter of Henry VIII, who defeated the Spanish Armada in 1588.

tossups.p: A victory at the Battle of Gravelines [“GRAV-uh-leen”] let this monarch’s navy and a timely storm scatter a huge invasion fleet in 1588. Plots against this monarch included the Ridolfi conspiracy and the Throckmorton conspiracy, the latter uncovered by her spymaster, Francis Walsingham.
tossups.r: Catholic conspirators wanted to replace her with her own prisoner and cousin, Mary, Queen of Scots. For 10 points, name this Tudor monarch, a daughter of Henry VIII known as the “Virgin Queen.”

tossups.p: This monarch signed the Treaty of Nonsuch to send English troops under Robert Dudley to aid Dutch rebels fighting Spain. She later ordered the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots for her role in the Babington Plot, a conspiracy aimed at this monarch’s own life.
tossups.r: This monarch was succeeded by Mary’s son, James I, the first Stuart king of England. For 10 points, name this Tudor queen, daughter of Anne Boleyn, nicknamed the “Virgin Queen.”

tossups.p: This monarch sent her favorite, Robert Dudley, to help Dutch forces resist Spain’s Duke of Parma, and later had her own former favorite, the Earl of Essex, executed for leading a failed rebellion. Under this monarch, the Thirty-Nine Articles officially defined the Church of England’s Protestant beliefs.

tossups.r: Francis Drake helped this ruler defeat a fleet nicknamed “Invincible” off the English coast in 1588. For 10 points, name this queen, a daughter of Anne Boleyn who ruled England for 44 years.

tossups.p: Playwrights William Shakespeare and Christopher Marlowe both wrote during this monarch’s reign, a cultural golden age now named for her. Sir Walter Raleigh named a North American colony “Virginia” in this unmarried monarch’s honor, hoping to flatter her with a nod to her most famous nickname.
tossups.r: That colony, founded on Roanoke Island, mysteriously disappeared a few years later. For 10 points, name this English queen whose 44-year reign is called the Elizabethan Era.

tossups.p: Edmund Spenser dedicated his epic poem _The Faerie Queene_ to this monarch, allegorizing her as the title character. Painters produced several famous portraits of this ruler, including one showing her hand resting on a globe to celebrate her navy’s 1588 victory over Spain.
tossups.r: That victory came against the Spanish Armada sent by King Philip II. For 10 points, name this English queen, daughter of Henry VIII, whose reign is called a golden age for English literature.

tossups.p: This monarch’s mother was executed on her father’s orders when this future ruler was only two years old, and she was declared illegitimate soon after. Despite that rocky start, she survived imprisonment in the Tower of London under her half-sister’s reign before finally taking the throne in 1558.
tossups.r: She ruled for the next 44 years without ever marrying. For 10 points, name this daughter of Anne Boleyn and Henry VIII, nicknamed the “Virgin Queen.”

tossups.p: In 1588, this monarch addressed her assembled troops at Tilbury while England still feared a Spanish invasion, delivering one of the most quoted speeches in English history. She told her soldiers she had come among them not for recreation, but resolved to live and die among them all.
tossups.r: By then, the Royal Navy and storms were already scattering Spain’s “Invincible” Armada. For 10 points, name this Tudor queen who ruled England from 1558 to 1603.

tossups.p: This monarch’s government passed the Thirty-Nine Articles, permanently establishing a moderate Protestant settlement for the English church. Decades later, she had the Earl of Essex, once a favorite courtier, executed after he led a failed uprising against her in London.
tossups.r: Essex had previously commanded failed military campaigns in Ireland on her behalf. For 10 points, name this queen, a daughter of Anne Boleyn who never married.

tossups.p: This monarch’s government drew up detailed plans to defend the English coastline with a chain of warning beacons, ready to light if Spanish ships were sighted. Her cousin Mary, Queen of Scots, had already been executed the year before for plotting against her in the Babington conspiracy.
tossups.r: Those beacons were lit when the Armada was sighted, but the Royal Navy and bad weather stopped any invasion. For 10 points, name this queen who ruled England during that 1588 victory.

tossups.p: Historians often call this monarch’s 44-year reign a golden age, pointing to English exploration, a flourishing of drama and poetry, and a newly confident Protestant Church of England. She balanced Catholic and Protestant factions at home while facing down the most powerful Catholic empire in Europe abroad.
tossups.r: Her famous victory over the Spanish Armada in 1588 became the defining moment of her reign. For 10 points, name this last Tudor monarch, daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn.

trap.title: Which Elizabeth? Which Mary?
trap.body: England has had two Queen Elizabeths, and real tossups explicitly say “do not accept Elizabeth II” for this earlier queen. This monarch is also easy to confuse with her own relatives: her father Henry VIII, her half-siblings Edward VI and Mary I, and her prisoner and rival Mary, Queen of Scots, whom she eventually had executed.
trap.fix: Spanish Armada, the Virgin Queen, Tilbury, and a 44-year unmarried reign mean this Elizabeth. A reigning queen with Prince Charles or Princess Diana means Elizabeth II. Six wives mean Henry VIII; a brief Catholic restoration means Mary I; a beheaded Scottish rival means Mary, Queen of Scots.

topics.name: Holy Roman Empire
topics.kicker: Elective empire at Europe’s center · From Charlemagne to Napoleon
topics.briefing: On Christmas Day in the year 800, Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king Charlemagne as emperor, reviving the idea of Rome in Western Europe. The empire that grew from his legacy covered much of what’s now Germany, Austria, and beyond, but its leading princes elected each new emperor rather than passing the crown father to son. Voltaire later joked that it was “neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire” — yet it lasted until Napoleon forced its last emperor to dissolve it in 1806.

tossups.p: On Christmas Day in the year 800, Pope Leo III crowned a Frankish king as emperor of this realm, reviving a title that had lapsed in Western Europe for centuries. Historians usually date this institution’s true founding to 962, though, when Otto I was crowned by a different pope.
tossups.r: Seven Prince-Electors eventually gained the right to choose each new ruler of this realm rather than passing the crown by birth. For 10 points, name this Central European empire that lasted, in some form, from Charlemagne to Napoleon.

tossups.p: The Golden Bull of 1356, issued by Emperor Charles IV, formally fixed the number of princes who could choose this realm’s ruler at seven. Those Prince-Electors met along with other princes and free cities in an assembly called the Imperial Diet to handle this realm’s affairs.
tossups.r: Unlike most kingdoms, this realm’s crown was elective rather than strictly hereditary. For 10 points, name this sprawling Central European empire, dissolved in 1806, that was once ruled by Charlemagne and Charles V.

tossups.p: A long fight over who could appoint bishops within this realm, called the Investiture Controversy, ended when Emperor Henry V and Pope Calixtus II signed the Concordat of Worms in 1122 as a compromise. Decades later, Frederick Barbarossa [“BAR-buh-ROH-suh”] fought the Lombard League, a group of Italian cities backed by the Papacy.
tossups.r: Barbarossa’s forces lost to that league at the Battle of Legnano in 1176. For 10 points, name this empire, centered on medieval Germany, whose rulers often clashed with the pope.

tossups.p: In 1521, this realm’s ruler summoned a rebellious monk to the Diet of Worms and then declared him an outlaw after he refused to recant his teachings. Friendly nobles then staged a fake kidnapping of that monk, Martin Luther, hiding him at Wartburg Castle for his own safety.
tossups.r: Luther’s ideas later split this realm’s princes into the Catholic side and the Protestant Schmalkaldic League, who fought a war against their own emperor. For 10 points, name this Central European empire that Charles V ruled during the Reformation.

tossups.p: One ruler of this realm inherited so many Habsburg and Spanish territories that his lands were said to never see a sunset, and he simultaneously reigned in Spain as King Charles I. After decades of war and religious conflict, that ruler abdicated in 1556, splitting his holdings between his son and his brother.
tossups.r: His brother Ferdinand I inherited this realm’s throne, while his son Philip II took the Spanish crown. For 10 points, name this empire, whose electors had chosen Charles V as ruler in 1519.

tossups.p: The Thirty Years’ War, a brutal conflict fought mostly within this realm’s borders, finally ended with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. That settlement recognized the Swiss Confederacy and the Dutch Republic as fully independent of this realm’s authority.
tossups.r: The peace also confirmed that each prince within this realm could set his own territory’s official religion. For 10 points, name this empire, whose power declined sharply after this devastating war.

tossups.p: After crushing Austrian and Russian forces at the Battle of Austerlitz in 1805, Napoleon organized many of this realm’s western territories into a new Confederation of the Rhine. Facing that pressure, Emperor Francis II dissolved this realm entirely the following year.
tossups.r: Francis had already created a separate Austrian imperial title for himself in 1804, anticipating that end. For 10 points, name this thousand-year-old empire, later nicknamed the “First Reich,” which Napoleon finally brought down in 1806.

tossups.p: Members of the Habsburg family held this realm’s throne almost without interruption from 1438 until its final dissolution, with one brief exception when a Bavarian Wittelsbach [“VIT-els-bahk”] prince took the title in the 1740s. This realm’s electors formally chose each new emperor at Frankfurt.
tossups.r: Despite the family’s dominance, every Habsburg ruler technically had to be elected rather than simply inheriting the office. For 10 points, name this Central European empire, nicknamed the “First Reich.”

tossups.p: A period with no effectively recognized ruler, called the Great Interregnum, left this realm in near chaos during the 1250s and 1260s after the fall of the Hohenstaufen [“HOH-en-shtow-fen”] dynasty. Electors finally ended that crisis in 1273 by choosing Rudolf of Habsburg, launching his family’s long rise to power.
tossups.r: Rudolf became the first Habsburg to hold this realm’s throne. For 10 points, name this Central European empire, whose crown the Habsburgs would later hold for centuries.

tossups.p: In 955, a king of this realm smashed an invading Magyar army at the Battle of Lechfeld [“LEKH-felt”], ending decades of raids into Central Europe. Seven years later, Pope John XII crowned that king, Otto, as emperor, an event many historians treat as this institution’s true beginning.
tossups.r: Otto’s coronation came more than a century and a half after Charlemagne’s own crowning on Christmas Day, 800. For 10 points, name this empire that Otto the Great is sometimes called the first true emperor of.

tossups.p: Dozens of “free imperial cities” within this realm answered directly to the emperor rather than to any local duke or bishop, giving them unusual independence in trade and local government. Together with princes and church leaders, representatives of these cities met in the Imperial Diet to debate this realm’s laws.
tossups.r: Hamburg and Frankfurt were among the most powerful of these self-governing cities. For 10 points, name this loosely organized Central European empire.

tossups.p: The French writer Voltaire famously joked that this realm was “neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire,” mocking how little real power its emperor held over its many separate princes. Despite that mockery, this loose confederation of states endured for roughly a thousand years.
tossups.r: Pressure from Napoleon finally ended it in 1806, after centuries of Habsburg rule. For 10 points, name this empire whose name promised more unity than it ever actually had.

tossups.p: A heraldic design called the Quaternion Eagle displayed the coats of arms of this realm’s many territories across the feathers of a double-headed eagle. Its later emperors flew a black double-headed eagle on a gold banner as this realm’s symbol.
tossups.r: A double-headed eagle later appeared on the coat of arms of the Austrian Empire long after this realm ended. For 10 points, name this empire, whose symbols outlived its 1806 dissolution.

tossups.p: This realm had no single fixed capital; its rulers instead moved between residences like Vienna, Prague, and Aachen, while the Prince-Electors traditionally gathered at Frankfurt to choose each new emperor. A separate imperial court, the Reichskammergericht [“RIKES-kammer-gericht”], handled legal disputes between this realm’s many territories.
tossups.r: This fragmented structure let hundreds of small states and free cities govern themselves with real independence. For 10 points, identify this loosely unified Central European empire.

tossups.p: For roughly a thousand years, this realm stood at the center of European politics without ever becoming a single unified nation-state, instead remaining a patchwork of kingdoms, duchies, and free cities loosely bound under one elected emperor. Its emperors were crowned by the pope for much of its history, linking this realm closely to the Catholic Church.
tossups.r: It was later nicknamed the “First Reich,” though it ended decades before any Second or Third Reich existed. For 10 points, name this empire that lasted from around 800 until Napoleon forced its dissolution in 1806.

trap.title: Not Charlemagne, Rome, or Austria
trap.body: This empire overlaps with several separate quiz bowl answers. Charlemagne and Otto the Great are specific emperors, not the empire itself, and Charles V and Napoleon are rulers connected to its high point and its end. The ancient Roman Empire and the later Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire share part of the name but are entirely different states, and the Austrian Empire that Francis II created in 1804 explicitly replaced this one — one real answer line for “Austrian Empire” even says “do not accept or prompt on Holy Roman Empire.”
trap.fix: Prince-Electors, the Imperial Diet, Charlemagne’s legacy, and an 1806 dissolution forced by Napoleon mean this empire. A single all-powerful Caesar means ancient Rome. A Germany united under Bismarck in 1871 means the German Empire instead.

topics.kicker: A potato blight that starved Ireland · Mass death and emigration
topics.briefing: When a water mold began rotting Ireland’s potato crop in 1845, the island’s poor lost their main food source. Over the next several years, about a million Irish men, women, and children died of starvation and disease, and roughly a million more fled overseas, many in crowded, disease-ridden “coffin ships.” The famine emptied whole villages and helped send waves of Irish immigrants to cities like Boston and New York.

Parliament’s disciplined New Model Army, built by Oliver Cromwell and Thomas Fairfax, crushed the king’s Cavaliers, and in 1649 Charles became the only English king ever put on trial and executed. tossups.p: The first major battle of this conflict, fought at Edgehill in 1642, ended without a clear winner on either side. This conflict began partly because the king at its center believed he answered only to God and could rule without Parliament’s consent.
tossups.r: In 1649, that king was put on trial and executed. For 10 points, name this 17th-century English conflict.

tossups.p: Just before this conflict began, the king personally marched into the House of Commons to arrest five members of Parliament, who had already fled. Years of royal taxes like ship money, raised without Parliament’s approval, had already angered many of the king’s subjects.
tossups.r: Parliament’s New Model Army later won this conflict at the Battle of Naseby. For 10 points, name this English war between king and Parliament.

tossups.p: Scotland’s Bishops’ Wars over a new prayer book forced the king to recall Parliament for money shortly before this conflict began. An eleven-year stretch of personal royal rule without Parliament came just before that.
tossups.r: This conflict split the country into Roundheads and Cavaliers. For 10 points, name this 17th-century war that led to a king’s execution.

tossups.p: Royalist cavalry commander Prince Rupert of the Rhine surrendered the city of Bristol during this conflict, leading to his court-martial. Rupert’s own cavalry had earlier been routed by Oliver Cromwell’s horsemen at one battle in the north.
tossups.r: This conflict eventually led to Oliver Cromwell ruling as Lord Protector. For 10 points, name this conflict between the king’s Cavaliers and Parliament’s Roundheads.

tossups.p: At one 1644 battle in this conflict, the Marquess of Newcastle’s “Whitecoats” infantry made a famous last stand after a long siege of the city of York. Prince Rupert commanded the king’s cavalry at that same battle, Marston Moor.
tossups.r: During this conflict, the king was tried and executed in 1649. For 10 points, name this English war.

tossups.p: After his cavalry was outflanked at Marston Moor, Prince Rupert reportedly hid in a bean field to escape capture during this conflict. Later in this conflict, Pride’s Purge removed moderate members from the Long Parliament, leaving only a smaller “Rump Parliament.”
tossups.r: Parliament’s New Model Army secured victory in this conflict. For 10 points, name this 17th-century English war.

tossups.p: A siege of a royal weapons store at Hull marked the opening moves of this conflict in 1642. Oliver Cromwell’s own disciplined cavalry regiment earned the nickname “Ironsides” during this conflict.
tossups.r: It eventually pitted Roundheads against Cavaliers. For 10 points, name this English conflict that led to a king’s execution.

tossups.p: The king’s advisor Thomas Wentworth, Earl of Strafford, was executed for treason just before this conflict began, an attempt to calm tensions that failed. Years into this conflict, the Self-Denying Ordinance forced most sitting politicians to give up their military commands.
tossups.r: One exception to that ordinance, Oliver Cromwell, helped win this conflict at the Battle of Naseby. For 10 points, name this English war.

tossups.p: Neutral local militias called Clubmen tried to protect their villages from both sides during this conflict. An eleven-year period without any Parliament at all, sometimes called the king’s “Personal Rule,” had helped cause this conflict.
tossups.r: It eventually led to Oliver Cromwell ruling England as Lord Protector. For 10 points, name this 17th-century conflict.

tossups.p: Campaigns tied to this conflict included harsh sieges of the Irish towns of Wexford and Drogheda [“DRAH-ed-uh”] in 1649. A short second round of this conflict in 1648 included an invasion of England by Scottish “Engagers” on the king’s behalf.
tossups.r: This conflict’s first round had already ended with the king’s defeat. For 10 points, name this English war that brought about King Charles the First’s execution.

tossups.p: Radical soldiers called Levellers argued for a wider right to vote during this conflict’s Putney Debates. Earlier, the Protestation of 1641 had members of Parliament swear to defend the Protestant religion and Parliament’s privileges, shortly before this conflict broke out.
tossups.r: Parliament’s New Model Army decided this conflict at the Battle of Naseby. For 10 points, name this English war.

tossups.p: A third round of this conflict ended when Oliver Cromwell defeated the former king’s son at the Battle of Worcester in 1651. Nine years after that, the monarchy was restored and Charles the Second finally took the throne his father had lost.
tossups.r: That father had been executed partway through this conflict. For 10 points, name this English war between Roundheads and Cavaliers.

tossups.p: This conflict’s opening moves included a siege of a weapons depot at Hull in 1642, before the first major battle at Edgehill ended in a draw. The king at the center of this conflict believed in his divine right to rule without Parliament’s consent.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this English conflict in which the New Model Army defeated the king’s Cavaliers.

tossups.p: Years of royal taxes raised without Parliament’s approval, like ship money, helped cause this conflict, as did a list of grievances called the Grand Remonstrance. The king at the center of this conflict also tried and failed to arrest five members of Parliament in person.
tossups.r: This conflict led to that king’s execution in 1649. For 10 points, name this English war.

tossups.p: This conflict’s three rounds of fighting stretched from a draw at Edgehill in 1642 to Oliver Cromwell’s victory over the old king’s son at Worcester in 1651. In between, Parliament’s New Model Army won decisively at the Battle of Naseby.
tossups.r: It ended the reign, and the life, of King Charles the First. For 10 points, name this 17th-century English war between Parliament and the crown.

trap.title: A war, not a person
trap.body: Real tossups spend most of their clues on Charles I and Oliver Cromwell, but “name this conflict” wants the war itself, not either man. Don’t confuse this war with the later, mostly bloodless Glorious Revolution (1688), which removed a different king (James II), or with the much earlier Wars of the Roses, another English civil war fought more than a century earlier over the crown itself.
trap.fix: “Name this conflict” or “this war” wants the English Civil War. “Name this king” wants Charles I; “name this general” or “this Lord Protector” wants Oliver Cromwell. Naseby and Marston Moor are battles within it, not the war’s own name.

topics.briefing: Marie Antoinette arrived in France at just fourteen to marry the future king and seal an alliance between Austria and France. trap.body: Russia later had a Peter II and a Peter III (Catherine the Great’s husband, overthrown in her coup), so always say the number or “the Great.” Don’t confuse this reformer with Ivan the Terrible, an earlier tsar also known by a dramatic nickname, or with Catherine the Great herself, who ruled decades later and has no blood tie to him (she married his grandson). In Great Northern War clues, Charles the Twelfth is the Swedish king on the other side, not this ruler.
trap.fix: The beard tax, the Grand Embassy, founding Saint Petersburg, and the Table of Ranks all mean Peter the Great. Clues about the Partitions of Poland or Pugachev’s Rebellion mean Catherine the Great instead. Say “Peter the Great” or “Peter the First,” not just “Peter.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Peter the Great (accept Peter I; prompt on Peter alone)
